patient.name: Maria Guzman
patient.chiefComplaint: 39 weeks pregnant, strong urge to push, contractions very close together

history.hpi: G2P1 at 39 weeks gestation. Labor started about 90 minutes ago and progressed unusually fast for her second pregnancy. Contractions are now less than 2 minutes apart and she reports an overwhelming urge to push and a feeling that the baby is coming now.
pastMedical: Prior uncomplicated vaginal delivery 2 years ago
history.events: Rapid onset of active labor at home; husband called 911 when patient stated the baby was coming

scene.dispatch: 29-year-old female, pregnant, in labor, contractions close together, residence
scene.location: Single-family home, living room, patient on the floor on a folded blanket at husband's direction
scene.safety: No hazards to crew noted; adequate space and lighting available
scene.bystanders: Husband present and coaching patient's breathing
visualCues: Patient in semi-reclined position with knees bent, visibly bearing down
Bag packed by the door — clearly prepared for imminent transport
Husband timing contractions on his phone, less than 2 minutes apart

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 29-year-old G2P1 female at 39 weeks with crowning visible and strong, frequent contractions. Delivery is clearly imminent.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Nonlabored between contractions, breath-holding during pushing
otherFindings: Contractions less than 2 minutes apart, strong
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "The baby's coming right now, I can't stop it!"

transitions.condition: Crew recognizes imminent delivery and prepares to support a slow, controlled delivery of the head and body rather than transporting.

phases.name: Controlled delivery performed
phases.description: Crew supports the infant's head with gentle counterpressure to prevent explosive delivery, checks for a nuchal cord, and guides delivery of the anterior and posterior shoulders.
phases.triggerCondition: With crowning visible and delivery clearly imminent, the crew commits to delivering on scene, applying gentle counterpressure to control the head's delivery and checking for a nuchal cord before proceeding.

otherFindings: Head delivered with gentle counterpressure, no nuchal cord present
Anterior shoulder delivering with gentle downward guidance
No tearing or excessive bleeding noted
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Oh god, oh god, is the head out?"

expectedActions.shortAction: Support head with gentle counterpressure for slow, controlled delivery
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Delivery should be controlled to allow a slow controlled delivery of infant – This will prevent injury to mother. Support the infant's head as needed and apply gentle counterpressure to help prevent the head from suddenly popping out
expectedActions.rationale: Prevents maternal perineal trauma from an uncontrolled, explosive delivery.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check for nuchal cord after head delivers; slip over head if present
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check for nuchal cord (i.e., around the baby's neck). If present, slip it over the head. If unable to free the cord from the neck, double clamp the cord and cut between the clamps
expectedActions.rationale: An unrecognized nuchal cord can obstruct delivery of the body or cause cord compression.

expectedActions.shortAction: Guide head down for anterior shoulder, then up for posterior shoulder
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Grasping the head with hand over the ears, gently guide head down to allow delivery of the anterior shoulder. Gently guide the head up to allow delivery of the posterior shoulder
expectedActions.rationale: Correct sequencing safely delivers each shoulder in turn without excessive traction.

transitions.condition: The remainder of the infant delivers slowly following the shoulders; crew proceeds directly to newborn stabilization and APGAR scoring.

phases.name: Newborn dried, warmed, and scored
phases.description: Newborn delivers with a strong cry and good tone. Crew dries, warms, and stimulates the infant, delays cord clamping appropriately, and calculates APGAR scores at 1 and 5 minutes.
phases.triggerCondition: Following delivery of the body, the newborn immediately cries vigorously with good tone and color, meeting criteria for routine care rather than resuscitation.

otherFindings: Newborn crying vigorously, good tone, pink centrally with acrocyanosis
Cord clamped and cut after approximately 1 minute
Newborn dried, warmed, and placed skin-to-skin on maternal chest
APGAR 9 at 1 minute (1 point off for acrocyanosis)
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can't believe it, is my baby okay? Let me see her!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Do not routinely suction infant's airway, even with bulb syringe
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Do not routinely suction the infant's airway (even with a bulb syringe) during delivery
expectedActions.rationale: Routine suctioning of a vigorous newborn provides no benefit and can cause vagally-mediated bradycardia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Clamp cord in two places about 5-6 inches from abdomen after 1 minute; cut between clamps
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: After 1 minute, clamp cord about 5–6 inches from the abdomen with two clamps; cut the cord between the clamps
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed cord clamping improves neonatal outcomes when resuscitation is not needed.

expectedActions.shortAction: Dry, warm, and stimulate infant; wrap in towel and place on maternal chest
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Dry, warm, and stimulate infant, wrap in towel and place on maternal chest unless resuscitation needed
expectedActions.rationale: Prevents neonatal hypothermia, a major driver of adverse outcomes in newborns.

expectedActions.shortAction: Calculate APGAR score at 1 and 5 minutes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Record APGAR scores at 1 and 5 minutes once neonate is stabilized
expectedActions.rationale: Standardized documentation of newborn transition status for the receiving team.
